Good morning, students. This is a reminder from Career Services. Our mock interview week begins on Monday. Volunteers from local companies will conduct twenty-minute practice interviews and give you written feedback. Spaces are limited, so please register through the student portal by this Friday. When you register, you'll be asked to upload a real job advertisement that interests you, so that your interviewer can ask relevant questions. Business dress is recommended but not required.

Before you leave, one note about Thursday. We'll be meeting in the materials lab in the engineering building, not here, because we're going to watch a glass tempering demonstration. Because the furnaces run extremely hot, closed-toe shoes are required. If you show up in sandals, the technicians won't let you in, and I can't make exceptions. Also, the lab only holds about thirty people, so the demonstration will run twice, at ten and at eleven. Your group assignments are on the course website. Please check which session you're in, because if both groups come at ten, nobody will see anything.

Today we're going to talk about why ordinary glass breaks the way it does, and how engineers make it stronger. If you look at glass under a powerful microscope, you'll see that its surface is covered in tiny scratches and flaws, far too small to notice with your eyes. When you bend a sheet of glass, the stress concentrates at the tips of these flaws, and a crack can spread from one of them almost instantly. So in practice, glass is much weaker than its chemistry would suggest. One solution is tempering. The glass is heated until it's almost soft, and then the outer surfaces are cooled very rapidly with jets of air. The outside hardens first, while the inside is still hot. As the inside cools, it shrinks and pulls on the outer layer, squeezing it. That squeezing, or compression, makes it much harder for surface cracks to open. Tempered glass can be several times stronger than ordinary glass. And there's another benefit. When it does break, it shatters into small, rounded pieces rather than long, sharp blades. That's why it's used in car side windows and shower doors. The tradeoff is that you can't cut tempered glass after it's made. Any attempt to cut it releases the stress, and the whole sheet falls apart. So it has to be cut to its final shape before tempering.

Let's go back to the goldsmiths of seventeenth-century London, because they help explain how modern banking works. Wealthy merchants needed somewhere safe to keep their gold, and goldsmiths already had strong vaults. So merchants deposited their gold and received a written receipt. Before long, people realized it was easier to pay each other by handing over these receipts than by fetching the gold itself. The receipts started to circulate almost like paper money. Here's where it gets interesting. The goldsmiths noticed that on any given day, only a small fraction of depositors actually came to withdraw their gold. Most of it just sat in the vault. So they began lending part of it out and charging interest, while keeping enough on hand to meet normal withdrawals. This is the basic idea behind what's now called fractional reserve banking. Of course, the system depended entirely on trust. If too many depositors suspected that their goldsmith couldn't pay, they'd all rush to withdraw at once, and even a well-run goldsmith would fail, simply because the gold was out on loan. That's essentially a bank run. In sixteen seventy-two, when the king stopped repaying loans that goldsmiths had made to the government, several of them collapsed for exactly this reason. Keep that in mind when we discuss deposit insurance next week.

Did you know that some plants can warn each other? When an animal eats the leaves of certain plants, the plants make a special smell. Other plants nearby notice this smell. Then they start to make their leaves taste bad, so animals will not want to eat them. Scientists first saw this in trees in the nineteen eighties. At first, many people did not believe it. But now scientists have seen it in many kinds of plants, such as tomatoes and corn. One day, farmers may use this idea to protect their crops without chemicals.

Your brain changes every time you learn something new. Inside your brain are billions of cells called neurons. When you practice a skill, like playing the piano, the neurons used for that skill connect more strongly. That is why practice makes things easier. If you stop practicing, some of those connections become weaker. Scientists used to think that only children's brains could change like this. Now we know that adult brains can change too. So it is never too late to learn a new language or a musical instrument.

Yes. I followed the protocol exactly. I damaged leaves on half the bean plants and measured defense compounds in the untouched plants next to them. But I didn't find any difference between those plants and the controls.
Where were the control plants?
On the same bench, about two meters away.
And was the greenhouse ventilation on?
It's always on. The fans run constantly in the summer.
Then that may be your answer. Those airborne signals are pretty dilute. With fans moving air around the whole room, your controls may have been exposed to the same compounds as the test plants.
So my controls weren't really controls.

Possibly. It's not a wasted experiment, though. A null result with a clear explanation is still worth writing up. But if you want to test the effect properly, you'd need to separate the groups, maybe in sealed chambers.
The department has a few of those, but they're booked through the end of the month.
Then put your name on the list, and in the meantime, write up what you have. Include the ventilation issue in your discussion section.

Attention, graduating seniors. Career Services has received a number of questions about the new employer verification process, so here's a quick clarification. Starting this semester, every job posting on the university's career portal will be reviewed before it goes live, which means new listings may take up to three business days to appear. This doesn't affect postings that are already on the site. We've introduced this step after several students reported postings from organizations that turned out not to exist. If you're ever asked to pay a fee to apply, or to provide your bank details before an interview, please don't respond. Report the posting to us instead. Legitimate employers will never ask you to do either of those things.

I want to look at a striking case of neuroplasticity: what happens in the brains of people who are blind from birth. The visual cortex, at the back of the brain, normally processes information from the eyes. You might expect that, without visual input, this region would simply sit idle. But brain imaging shows the opposite. In people who were born blind, the visual cortex becomes highly active when they read Braille with their fingertips, and even during certain language tasks. In other words, a region we label visual has been recruited for touch and language. Now, the obvious question is whether this activity actually does anything, or whether it's just a side effect. One clever way to test it is to briefly disrupt the visual cortex using magnetic stimulation. When researchers did this in blind participants, their Braille reading became noticeably less accurate. In sighted participants, the same stimulation had no effect on reading by touch. So the activity seems to be functionally important. There's an important limitation, though. This kind of reorganization appears to be much more extensive in people who lost their sight early in life. In people who became blind as adults, the visual cortex is recruited to a lesser degree. So plasticity is real, but its extent depends heavily on timing.

Today I want to talk about an innovation that made long-distance trade possible: the bill of exchange, which Italian merchant bankers developed in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Imagine a wool merchant in Florence who wants to buy cloth in Bruges. Carrying chests of coins across the Alps was slow and dangerous. Instead, he'd pay a Florentine banker, who would write a bill instructing the banker's partner in Bruges to pay the equivalent in local currency. The merchant's agent would collect the money on arrival. No coins had to cross the mountains at all. But there's a subtler point here. The Church at the time prohibited usury, which meant charging interest on a loan. Bills of exchange offered a way around this. Because the bill involved converting one currency into another, and some time passed before payment, bankers could build a profit into the exchange rate. Technically, it was a currency transaction, not a loan, so it didn't count as interest. Historians still debate how much the system existed mainly for trade and how much it existed to disguise lending. My own view is that you can't separate the two neatly. The same document often did both jobs. In any case, bills of exchange created networks of trust between cities that later formed the backbone of international banking.

tasks.title: Read an Academic Passage
tasks.text:
The Changing Brain

For much of the twentieth century, neuroscientists believed that the adult brain was essentially fixed. Neurons, it was thought, formed their connections during childhood, and after that the brain could only decline. This view has since been overturned. Research has shown that the brain reorganizes itself throughout life in response to experience, a capacity known as neuroplasticity.

One striking demonstration came from studies of London taxi drivers, who must memorize thousands of streets before receiving a license. Brain scans revealed that the posterior hippocampus, a region involved in spatial memory, was larger in experienced drivers than in comparable adults. Because the difference grew with years on the job, researchers concluded that intensive practice had likely altered the drivers' brains, rather than people with larger hippocampi simply choosing the job.

Neuroplasticity is not limitless, however. Changes tend to be greatest when a skill is practiced intensively and repeatedly, and some abilities, such as acquiring a native-like accent in a new language, appear harder to develop after adolescence. Moreover, plasticity works in both directions: connections that are rarely used may weaken over time.

tasks.title: Read an Academic Passage
tasks.text:
Do Plants Talk?

When a caterpillar chews a tomato leaf, the plant does more than repair the damage. It releases a blend of volatile organic compounds, airborne chemicals that can be detected by neighboring plants. In laboratory experiments, plants exposed to these compounds began producing defensive proteins before they themselves were attacked, as if they had been warned. Some researchers have described this as plant communication, and the metaphor has proved irresistible to journalists.

Other scientists urge caution. Communication, in the strict biological sense, implies that the sender benefits from transmitting the signal. Yet it is not obvious why a damaged plant would gain from alerting its competitors, which vie with it for light and nutrients. One alternative explanation is that the compounds are primarily a message from one part of the plant to another: because chemical signals travel slowly through a plant's vascular system, releasing them into the air may be a faster way to reach distant branches. On this view, neighbors are merely eavesdropping on a private conversation. Supporting this interpretation, the effect in many field studies is detectable only over short distances, often less than a meter, which is consistent with a signal intended for the plant's own tissues rather than for a wider audience.

email.title: Write an Email
email.subject: Feedback on my résumé
email.prompt:
Last week you attended a résumé workshop at your university's career center. At the end, the advisor, Mr. Okonkwo, offered to review your résumé and send you comments by email. You sent him your résumé the same day, but you have not received any feedback. You plan to apply for a summer internship that closes next Wednesday.

Write an email to Mr. Okonkwo. In your email, do the following:
- Mention something from the workshop that you found useful.
- Explain your situation.
- Ask for his help and suggest a way he could give it.

Use full sentences, and write as much as you can.
email.rubric: Task: polite follow-up email to a career advisor. Must cover all 3 bullets: (1) a specific useful point from the workshop, (2) the situation (resume sent, no reply yet, internship deadline next Wednesday), (3) a clear request plus a concrete suggestion (short meeting, drop-in visit, quick comments by a date). Look for a tactful tone that does not blame the advisor, greeting and sign-off, logical order, accurate grammar and precise vocabulary. Typical strong length 100-150 words.

discussion.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
discussion.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on education. Post a reply to the professor's question. In your reply, do these two things.
- State your view and back it up.
- Add something new to the thread, in your own words.
Aim for at least 100 words.

professor.name: Dr. Harlow
professor.text: Research on neuroplasticity shows that the brain can change throughout life, but some skills, such as speaking a language with a native-like accent, seem easier to develop when we are young. Because of this, some people argue that schools should start teaching a foreign language in the first year of primary school. Others say young children should focus on their first language and basic skills, and that foreign languages can be learned well later. Which view do you agree with, and why?

students.name: Priya
students.text: I think schools should start early. Children copy sounds easily and are not afraid of making mistakes. My cousin started English at six and now speaks it much more naturally than I do, even though I started at fourteen.

students.name: Lukas
students.text: I disagree. An hour or two a week in primary school is not enough to learn a language anyway. It would be better to spend that time on reading and math, and then teach languages more intensively when students are older and can study grammar seriously.

discussion.rubric: Task: academic discussion post, 100+ words. Look for a clear position, specific support (age and accent, amount of class time, motivation, cost, teacher quality), engagement with Priya's or Lukas's point that adds a new angle rather than repeating it, coherence, and varied accurate grammar and vocabulary.

interview.title: Take an Interview
interview.instructions: An interviewer will ask you four questions. There is no preparation time. You have 45 seconds to answer each question.
interview.context: You are joining a research study about how students prepare for their careers. A researcher will ask you some questions in a short online interview.

items.text: Thanks for taking part in this study about how people prepare for their careers. First, could you tell me what kind of work you hope to do in the future?
When people need career advice, some talk to family and friends, while others prefer professional advisors. Who would you go to for advice, and why?
Some people think it's better to stay in one job for a long time, while others think that changing jobs every few years helps people grow. What's your view?
Finally, some universities now require every student to complete an internship before graduating. Do you think internships should be required? Why or why not?
